Studies that evaluate a diagnostic test (often a screening instrument in psychiatry e.g. CAGE etc) generally evaluate the relationship between two phenomena – being positive for the standard diagnostic test vs. being positive for the evaluated screening test. These are generally cross sectional studies where the whole study sample can be classified into 4 groups A, B , C and D as follows • True positive = A, true negative = D • False positive = B, false negative = C Total number of subjects in the study is (A+B+C+D). This can be classified using the results of a gold standard test (comparator) and results of the test being evaluated (often a screening test). Some subjects will show a positive result for the gold standard test (the ones who are ‘really’ diseased: A+C) and others will not have the disease and so will be negative for the gold standard test (B+D). Among those who are really diseased i.e. the A+C group, only some will show positive result for the screening test. They are called true positives (A). Those who show negative result for the screening test but are really diseased constitute the false negative group(C). Among those who are not diseased i.e. the B+D group, only some will show a negative result for the screening test. They are called true negatives (D). Those who do not show positive result for the screening test but are really diseased constitute the false positive group(B). Studies that evaluate causation (often a screening instrument in psychiatry e.g. CAGE, etc.) generally evaluate the relationship between two phenomena – exposure and outcome. These are generally either case-control designs or cohort designs. Case%control,studies:, The total number of subjects in the study is (A+B+C+D). In case-control studies, the cases and controls are the definitive groups – hence the total sample can be classified accordingly to cases (A+C) and Controls (B+D). Among A+C cases, some would have been exposed to the causative agent under study (A) while others will remain unexposed (C). Similarly, among B+D controls, some would have been exposed (B) while the others will remain unexposed (D). Two groups: Four measures The two definitive groups can be described according to the odds and probabilities of exposure. Case exposure rate = A/A+C Control exposure rate = B/B+D Odds of exposure in cases: = number of exposed cases / number of non-exposed cases = A/C Odds of exposure in controls: = number of exposed controls / number of non-exposed controls = B/D Letter E below the 2X2 table reminds us to use Exposure measures in the first column. © SPMM Course Odds ratio This is given by the ratio of the odds of being exposed if you are a case rather than a control. OR = odds of exposure in cases/ odds of exposure in controls = (A/C)/(B/D) = AD/BC Note that if a disease is very rare (prevalence < 5% arbitrarily), then odds ratio approximates RR. OR can have values only between 0 and infinity (no negative values). Hence to calculate confidence intervals one needs to use log transformations. Cohort,studies:, An important advantage of cohort designs is that we can calculate risk rates from these studies. The risk is the probability of an event happening – in other words, the incidence rate of an outcome when a population of interest is observed for a period of time. Incidence needs prospective observation – hence cannot be obtained from case-control designs. The total number of subjects in the study is (A+B+C+D). In cohort studies, the exposed, and the non-exposed are the definitive groups – hence the total sample can be classified accordingly to exposure status as: exposed (A+B) and non-exposed (C+D). Among A+B exposed individuals, some will develop the expected disease (A) while others will remain healthy (B). Similarly, among C+D non-exposed individuals, many will remain healthy (D) while some may become unwell (C). Letter E below the 2X2 table reminds us to use Exposure measures in the first column. © SPMM Course Two groups: Four measures The two definitive groups can be described according to the odds and probabilities of developing the expected disease. • Absolute risk of disease in the exposed = A/A+B • Absolute risk of disease in the non-exposed = C/C+D • Odds of finding the disease among the exposed: = number of diseased individuals / number of non-diseased among the exposed = A/B • Odds of finding the disease among the non-exposed: = number of diseased individuals / number of non-diseased among the non- exposed = C/D OR = odds of the disease among the exposed/ odds of the disease among the non-exposed = (A/B)/(C/D) = AD/BC. Note that this measure is the same as the OR derived from a case-control design. Risk rates: Risk difference: This is the difference between two absolute risks described above in the two groups RD = AR exposed – AR non-exposed This is also called as absolute risk reduction (ARR: preferred term in clinical trials) or the Attributable Risk (preferred term in causal studies). Relative risk: The most important final estimate from most cohort studies is the relative risk. In cohort studies, RR can be calculated as the ratio of the disease (outcome) in the exposed to the disease in non-exposed RR = [A/ (A+B)] / [C / (C+D)] RR is the ratio between the probability of developing the disease if you are exposed to the probability of developing the disease if you are not. It is clinically more meaningful measure than the OR. It is also called as the risk ratio. Applying to local population: Population Attributable Risk: This is also called as the risk daddy by epidemiologists. It is a very useful public health measure. PAR is obtained by multiplying Attributable Risk by the proportion of the total population exposed to the studied causative agent. PAR provides the number of cases that could be eliminated by eradicating the exposure. PAR = ARR X Proportion exposed © SPMM Course OR and RR: Under certain situations, odds ratios become equivalent numerically to relative risks. Such a circumstance occurs when the probability of an event occurring is low. This has been called the rare disease assumption, with a probability (or prevalence) of less than 5% being a commonly used benchmark. However, when an event occurs more commonly, the odds ratio increases dramatically, even as the relative risk remains constant as shown below. Apart from case-control studies (and cohort studies), odds ratios are routinely used in analyses of dichotomous outcomes in clinical trials as they greatly facilitate statistical analyses. In chronic diseases such as schizophrenia, an important survival question relates to the risk of relapse/rehospitalisation when taking treatment. In addition, many events of interest such as medication discontinuation, self-harm and violence can be quantified when time-to-event is taken into consideration. A simple graphical method for doing this is plotting the time along x-axis and proportion surviving (i.e. not attaining) ‘an event’ is plotted along the y-axis. The event could be death, treatment response, relapse, etc. The cumulative probability of an individual remaining free of the event is displayed at each point. These curves have a stepped appearance, with each step taking place at a time of observation. These are called Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves. © SPMM Course ♣ If the study runs for a 5-year period, then not all subjects would have reached the outcome by that time. Hence, these observations are censored. They are called left censored if the observations began well after some events have occurred (missed past events) or right- censored if the observation was terminated before all events could be observed (missed future events). ♣ Due to censoring we often do not know the actual survival times beyond the end of the study period; so we cannot calculate the mean survival time of the whole group. However, we can determine median survival time, which corresponds to the survival time of 50 per cent of the observed sample. In the above figure, the median survival time is 24 months. At this time, half of the patients still survived. Obviously the median survival time can be calculated only if the observation was long enough for enough events to take place in half of the sample so that the Kaplan-Meier curve goes down far enough. ♣ Comparison of survival rates of two samples can be undertaken using log-rank test. It is a non-parametric test to analyze the difference between the survival curves of two groups. But the log-rank test cannot be used to account or adjust for effects of other variables such as confounders (because it is a univariate test). To study multiple variables one needs multivariate logistic Cox regression analysis (called as proportional hazard as it assumes that the effects of multiple variables are constant over a period of time – it is a semiparametric method). See the table below for further methods of analyzing survival data ♣ Log-rank test only informs whether significant differences are present or not by comparing two survival curves. It does not measure the magnitude of such differences. Hazard ratio gives the size of such differences. ♣ Mantel-Haenszel test could be used in life tables to study the effect of two binary independent variables (e.g. male vs. female and treatment vs. placebo) on the outcome. heading: Evaluating Prognosis — Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves
text:
Evaluating Prognosis
            Both cohort studies and RCTs are used for estimating the prognosis of clinical samples. In chronic diseases such as
     schizophrenia, an important survival question relates to the risk of relapse/rehospitalisation when taking treatment. In addition, many
     events of interest such as medication discontinuation, self-harm and violence can be quantified when time-to-event is taken into
     consideration.

     A simple graphical method for doing this is plotting the time along x-axis and proportion surviving (i.e. not attaining) ‘an event’ is
     plotted along the y-axis. The event could be death, treatment response, relapse, etc. The cumulative probability of an individual
     remaining free of the event is displayed at each point. These curves have a stepped appearance, with each step taking place at a time
     of observation. These are called Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves.

heading: Evaluating Prognosis — Censoring, Median Survival Time, Log-rank & Cox Regression
text:
♣   If the study runs for a 5-year period, then not all subjects would have reached the outcome by that time. Hence, these observations are
      censored. They are called left censored if the observations began well after some events have occurred (missed past events) or right-
      censored if the observation was terminated before all events could be observed (missed future events).

  ♣   Due to censoring we often do not know the actual survival times beyond the end of the study period; so we cannot calculate the mean
      survival time of the whole group. However, we can determine median survival time, which corresponds to the survival time of 50 per
      cent of the observed sample. In the above figure, the median survival time is 24 months. At this time, half of the patients still survived.
      Obviously the median survival time can be calculated only if the observation was long enough for enough events to take place in half of
      the sample so that the Kaplan-Meier curve goes down far enough.

  ♣   Comparison of survival rates of two samples can be undertaken using log-rank test. It is a non-parametric test to analyze the difference
      between the survival curves of two groups. But the log-rank test cannot be used to account or adjust for effects of other variables such
      as confounders (because it is a univariate test). To study multiple variables one needs multivariate logistic Cox regression analysis
      (called as proportional hazard as it assumes that the effects of multiple variables are constant over a period of time – it is a

  ♣   Log-rank test only informs whether significant differences are present or not by comparing two survival curves. It does not measure the

heading: 1. Are the results valid?
text: Was the sample of patients representative? First, deter- mine whether patients pass through some sort of filter before entering the study. If they do, the result is likely a sample that is systematically different from the underlying population of interest. Were the patients sufficiently similar to each other with respect to prognostic factors? Including different stages of disease in the cohort will make the survival estimates of the group not applicable to each group member. Was follow-up sufficiently complete? The larger the number of patients whose fate is unknown relative to the number who had the event of interest, the greater the threat to the validity. Were outcome criteria objective and unbiased? Outcome events may be objective and easily measured (eg, death), require some judgment (eg, myocardial infarction), or require considerable judgment and effort to measure (eg, disability, quality of life). Investigators should clearly specify and define their target outcomes and, whenever possible, they should base their criteria on objective measures.

Advantages of Meta-Analysis: Well-conducted meta-analyses have a number of important advantages over individual RCTs. 1. Increased power: The primary advantage of meta-analyses is an increase in statistical power over that of individual RCTs. 2. Clarify the direction of literature: Often, in a given area of interest, various RCTs may provide contradictory results, Meta-analysis can either reveal an underlying unifying conclusion among seemingly contradictory study findings, or explore the reasons for contradictions. Critically important aspects: 1. Methodologically rigorous meta-analytical techniques can be applied to suboptimal data leading to inconclusive results. No amount of statistical technique can improve the fundamental quality of the data being combined for the meta-analysis. This is sometimes referred to as garbage in-garbage out (GIGO) principle. 2. Publication bias occurs as studies that produce a statistically significant result are much more likely to be published than “negative” trials. This can lead to overestimating the effect of the intervention in the meta-analysis. To avoid or reduce the impact of this bias, one must systematically search for negative trials for inclusion in the meta-analysis.

Actually one would like to cover all relevant studies, but although the authors of the original studies are contacted for missing information, not all of them can send this information. 5. Differing statistic models. There are debates as to which statistical model is most suitable in which situation, even though often no relevant differences result from the choice in the case of robust data (apart from the different interpretation of absolute and relative risk reductions as explained above). It is a common practice to both fixed and random effect analyses in a given data set.

heading: 6. Inappropriate subgroup analyses
text: Exploring subgroup findings is a common feature of meta-analyses, sometimes as a way of explaining a failure to find any overall effect. A subset of studies or subgroups of patients may be analysed separately. While this approach may offer insights that can be tested in further RCTs, caution should be exercised in interpretation. Despite the underlying studies being randomised, this randomization and the subsequent likely balance between treated and control groups does not extend to subgroups defined after the fact. Thus, there is great potential for confounding and misleading findings.

heading: 7. Sensitivity analyses
text: (See ‘Secondary Research’ notes) The process of selection, inclusion and aggregation of data may affect the main findings in a meta-analysis. Hence meta-analysts commonly carry out some sensitivity analysis. This explores the ways in which the main findings are changed by varying the approach to aggregation. A good sensitivity analysis © SPMM Course should model the effect of excluding various categories of studies, e.g., unpublished studies or those of poor quality. It should also examine how consistent the results are across various subgroups. In meta-analyses without sensitivity analyses the reader has to make guesses about the likely impact of these important factors on the final results Questions)for)appraisal)of)a)meta0analysis:) (from Guyatt et al. JAMA series) Is the meta-analysis based on a written protocol that clearly outlines research question, primary and secondary outcomes, and inclusion and exclusion criteria? Has a thorough literature search been performed? Have different search engines (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane library, etc.) been used to identify relevant literature? Did the authors look for unpublished data, for negative studies, and for publications in non-English languages to minimise retrieval, language, and publication bias? Was a strategy to exclude individual studies clearly outlined in the publication? Did two investigators independently perform the quality assessment of the individual studies? Were sensitivity analyses performed? (Note that if the final estimate is standardised mean or Cohen’s d effect size, then the line of no difference will be placed on 0). On either side of this line, we have the two possible interpretations of the study results. If a study’s final point estimate (block or square) is on the right side of the line, then this will favour AP+AD. If it is on the left side, this will favour AP. If a study gives precise results (which happens especially if the sample size is large), then the length of this line will be shorter. Spiker study has a horizontal line whose right end cannot be shown in the plot – hence an arrow mark is placed: this is a sign of imprecision. Depending on the weight given to a study, the square will vary in size, bigger the square, greater the weight given to this study’s results. The actual weight is also denoted as the 5th column. The diamond lozenge is the pooled result. It will have no horizontal line (in fact, a very small line that is gobbled up by the arms of the lozenge ) as the pooled results have highest precision.
